title: 📚 Era 2 Works: The Medieval Age
subtitle: Verify publication dates, summaries, characters, storylines & exam traps for 59 works

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Caedmon’s Hymn

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: late 7th century (Sort Year: 650)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Caedmon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A nine line Old English hymn in which Caedmon praises God as Creator.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says fl. c. 7th century. Bede places the story in Hild's time at Whitby, about 657 to 680. The hymn is the earliest Old English poem with a secure early date. The oldest copies sit in 8th century manuscripts of Bede, including the Moore Bede. Bede finished the History in 731. That year is not the year of the hymn.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Caedmon (The cowherd at Whitby who sings the hymn after a dream); Dream visitor (The man in the dream who orders a song of creation); Abbess Hild (Head of Whitby, who tests the hymn and welcomes him as a monk)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
At a feast the harp comes toward Caedmon, and he leaves because he cannot sing.
In sleep a man asks him to sing of the beginning of created things.
He sings a short hymn on God, heaven, and the earth.
In the morning he tells the reeve, and Abbess Hild has scholars test him.
They find the gift holy, and he becomes a monk who versifies Scripture.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Battle of Maldon

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: after 991 (Sort Year: 991)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Beowulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Byrhtnoth and his loyal men die fighting Vikings at Maldon.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Oxford dates the battle to 991. The poem was made after that defeat. Cotton Otho A.xii burned in 1731. The text survives in a transcript, now Bodleian MS Rawlinson B.203.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Byrhtnoth (The English leader who refuses tribute and dies in battle); The Viking messenger (The raider who demands gold before the fight); Byrhtwold (An old retainer who urges the men to stand firm)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Vikings demand tribute, and Byrhtnoth refuses to pay.
He lets the raiders cross a narrow causeway to fight.
Byrhtnoth is killed, and some of his men run away.
Loyal retainers stay and choose death with their lord.
The fragment ends on their speeches of courage.

items.title: "The Dream of the Rood" (8th-10th century) — Anonymous — Beowulf

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Dream of the Rood

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 8th-10th century (Sort Year: 950)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Beowulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dreamer hears the Cross tell the story of the Crucifixion.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The full poem, 156 lines, is in the Vercelli Book, copied in the later 10th century. Shorter lines in runes appear on the Ruthwell Cross, often dated to the 8th century. The link between cross and book is debated.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Dreamer (The sinner who sees the vision and then prays); The Rood (The speaking Cross that tells of Christ's death); Christ (The young hero who climbs the Cross by his own will)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The dreamer sees a wondrous tree, bright with gold and blood.
The Cross speaks and tells how it was cut and raised.
Christ climbs upon it, and both are wounded and mocked.
Friends bury the Cross, and later it is honored as a relic.
The dreamer wakes and hopes for heaven through the Cross.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Seafarer

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: before c. 970 (Sort Year: 970)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Beowulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sailor describes hard voyages and chooses the heavenly journey.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Like The Wanderer, it survives in the Exeter Book of about 970. The year of composition is unknown. Bishop Leofric gave the book to Exeter, and he died in 1072.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Seafarer (A sailor speaker who weighs sea hardship against earthly joy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker tells of cold, lonely time at sea.
He contrasts the comfort of land with the pull of the waves.
He says earthly lords, gold, and friends will pass.
He urges the listener to fear God and live humbly.
The poem ends on the hope of heaven, not on fame.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Wanderer

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: before c. 970 (Sort Year: 970)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Beowulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An exile mourns his dead lord and a ruined heroic world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem survives only in the Exeter Book. Exeter Cathedral says a scribe wrote that book about 970. The poem is older than the book, but the exact year is unknown.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Wanderer (An exile who speaks of loss, ruin, and wisdom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A lonely speaker wakes and remembers his lost lord.
He recalls gift giving and joy in the hall.
He asks where the horse, the rider, and the giver have gone.
He looks at ruined walls where bright halls once stood.
He turns from earthly fame toward God's mercy.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 731 (Sort Year: 731)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Bede

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Latin history of the English church from Julius Caesar to the year 731.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Bede was then about 59. Some references say 731 or 732. The five books run from Caesar to 731. He dedicated the work to King Ceolwulf of Northumbria. An Old English translation was made later. It is no longer treated as King Alfred's own work.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bede (The monk who writes the history and closes it with his own life note); Gregory the Great (The pope whose letters and plan send Augustine to the English); Augustine of Canterbury (The missionary who reaches Kent in 597); Caedmon (The Whitby poet whose gift of song Bede records); King Edwin (The Northumbrian king whose council hears the parable of the sparrow)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Book 1 describes Britain and moves from Caesar to Augustine's mission in 597.
Later books follow the faith through Kent, Northumbria, and the other kingdoms.
The Synod of Whitby in 664 settles the Roman date of Easter.
Bede tells of holy lives, including Caedmon at Whitby and the sparrow in Edwin's hall.
Book 5 reaches Bede's own time, and he adds a short note on his life.

items.title: "Alfredian learning revival" (late 9th century) — King Alfred the Great

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Alfredian learning revival

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: late 9th century (Sort Year: 850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: King Alfred the Great

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Alfred's late reign plan to restore learning by teaching English and translating key books.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The revival belongs to his later reign, especially the 890s. Britannica says the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle began in his reign, about 890. The preface to Pastoral Care is the firmest text of the plan. Some scholars doubt that Alfred himself wrote every translation in the group.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: King Alfred (The king who plans schools and a set of English translations); Plegmund (Archbishop who helps with the books and receives a copy); Asser (Bishop named among Alfred's teachers and helpers); Grimbald and John (Priests from abroad who join the teaching circle)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Alfred recalls a time when England had wisdom, wealth, and peace.
He says that in his own day few people could read Latin, or even English.
He blames neglect, and he links the loss with the years of Viking attack.
He asks bishops to help train freeborn youth to read English, then Latin.
He gathers scholars and starts English versions of the books people most need.

items.title: "translation tradition including Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care" (c. 890-897) — King Alfred the Great

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: translation tradition including Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care

fields.label: Author
fields.value: King Alfred the Great

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Alfred's English version of Gregory's guide for bishops, sent out with a famous preface.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The English preface went to bishops whose dates overlap about 890 to 897. Plegmund became archbishop in 890. Hatton 20, sent to Worcester, was copied in Alfred's lifetime. The Latin original is Gregory's, not Alfred's. Scholars still debate how much Alfred wrote himself.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: King Alfred (Named speaker of the preface and sponsor of the English version); Gregory the Great (Author of the Latin Pastoral Care, a guide for bishops); Bishop Waerferth (Bishop of Worcester, named in the copy that still survives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gregory the Great wrote a Latin handbook on how bishops should care for souls.
Alfred's preface laments the fall of learning on both sides of the Humber.
He says he turned the book into English with help from four named teachers.
Each bishopric is to receive a copy, with a rich pointer called an aestel.
The Hatton 20 copy is addressed to Bishop Waerferth and marked for Worcester.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Christ II

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 9th century (Sort Year: 850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cynewulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A signed poem on Christ's Ascension, drawn mainly from a homily by Gregory the Great.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says probably 8th to 9th century. The signed poems are usually placed in the 9th century. Christ II is only the middle poem of the Christ group. Christ I and Christ III are not signed by him. The Exeter Book was copied in the later 10th century. That is the manuscript date, not the year of composition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Christ (The Lord who ascends and promises to remain with his people); The angels (Messengers who explain the ascent and warn of the last judgment); The disciples (Watchers who grieve as Christ is taken into the clouds)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Christ spends forty days on earth after rising, then ascends into heaven.
Angels tell the watchers that he will return to judge all deeds.
The poet praises the gifts God shares among people, including song and skill.
Six leaps of Christ run from the Incarnation to the Ascension.
Runes near the close spell Cynwulf and turn the mind toward Judgment.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Elene

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 9th century (Sort Year: 850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cynewulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Saint Helena, mother of Constantine, searches Jerusalem and finds the True Cross.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says probably 8th to 9th century. Elene is signed in runes and is usually placed in the 9th century. It is the last poem in the Vercelli Book, copied in the late 10th century. The Latin source is a legend of the finding of the cross, linked with the Acts of Cyriacus. The copy date is not the year of composition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Constantine (The emperor whose vision of the cross wins his battle); Elene (Helena, his mother, who leads the search for the True Cross); Judas Cyriacus (The man who reveals the cross, believes, and is renamed at baptism); Satan (The devil who rages when the true cross is revealed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Constantine sees a cross in the sky and defeats his enemies under that sign.
He sends his mother Elene with a troop to find the buried cross.
Judas refuses to speak, and she holds him without food until he yields.
Three crosses are dug up, and the true one raises a dead man.
Judas is baptized as Cyriacus.
The epilogue adds Cynewulf's runes and a vision of doom.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Juliana

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 9th century (Sort Year: 850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cynewulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The virgin Juliana refuses a pagan marriage and dies a martyr in Nicomedia.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says probably 8th to 9th century. Juliana is one of the four rune signed poems and is usually placed in the 9th century. The Exeter Book copy is dated about 970 to 990. About 130 lines are missing because a sheet was lost. The manuscript date is not the year of composition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Juliana (A Christian virgin of Nicomedia who chooses martyrdom); Eleusius (The pagan official who tries to marry her and then orders her death); Africanus (Her father, who gives Eleusius leave to punish her); A demon (A devil who enters the prison disguised as an angel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Under Maximian, Africanus pledges his daughter Juliana to the pagan Eleusius.
She refuses the marriage because she will not break faith with God.
Eleusius has her beaten and thrown into prison.
A demon visits her as an angel.
She seizes him and forces a confession.
Fire does not burn her.
She is beheaded, and the poem closes with runes.

items.title: "The Fates of the Apostles" (9th century) — Cynewulf

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Fates of the Apostles

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 9th century (Sort Year: 850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cynewulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short signed poem that lists how each of the twelve apostles died.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says probably 8th to 9th century. The Fates of the Apostles is signed in runes and is usually placed in the 9th century. It stands in the Vercelli Book, copied in the late 10th century. At 122 lines it is the shortest of the four signed poems. The manuscript date is not the year of composition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Cynewulf (The speaker who lists the apostles and asks for prayers); The twelve apostles (The missionaries whose travels and deaths the poem records)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet says he has heard of the bold deeds of the apostles.
He names their missions and the deaths they met in many lands.
The list works like a short martyrology for learners in a monastery.
He asks readers to pray for him when they hear the song.
Scattered runes at the end spell his name and speak of wealth that fails.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Catholic Homilies

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ælfric of Eynsham

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two series of English sermons on the Gospels, the saints, and Christian belief.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: 955 to c. 1010 is Aelfric's life, not the year of this book. Oxford dates the first series to about 989 and the second to 991 to 993. The prefaces address Sigeric, archbishop from 990 to 994. Exam lists often say about 990 to 995. That span covers the same work.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aelfric (The monk and mass priest who turns Latin teaching into English sermons); Archbishop Sigeric (Archbishop of Canterbury from 990 to 994, who receives the copies); The congregation (English hearers for whom each piece fits a day in the church year)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Each series holds about forty pieces for Sundays and feast days.
Aelfric explains readings, tells saint's lives, and teaches doctrine in plain English.
He sends copies to Archbishop Sigeric of Canterbury.
He says that, apart from Alfred's translations, English readers lacked sound teaching.
Later scribes mixed the two series, so few manuscripts keep either set whole.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Grammar

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 995 (Sort Year: 995)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ælfric of Eynsham

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Latin grammar explained in English, the first such book in medieval Europe.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: 955 to c. 1010 is his life span. Wikipedia places the Grammar, the Glossary, and the Colloquy around 995, after the two homily series. The Grammar is counted as the first Latin grammar in a medieval vernacular.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aelfric (The teacher who explains Latin grammar in English); His students (Boys who need English help before they can read Latin books)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After the Homilies, Aelfric turned to tools for students of Latin.
He first gathered a Latin grammar from Priscian and Donatus.
He then set that grammar out in English so boys could use it.
A glossary groups words by topic, and a Colloquy trains spoken Latin.
Together these books open the path from English reading into Latin.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lives of Saints

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ælfric of Eynsham

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English lives of saints honored in monasteries, written for two noble patrons.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: 955 to c. 1010 is his life span. Wikipedia dates the Lives to 996 to 997. Oxford gives a wider window, about 994 to 998, while he was still at Cerne. Both place the book after the Catholic Homilies and before he became abbot in 1005.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aelfric (The author, writing a third collection after the two homily series); Aethelweard (The noble patron who asks for these further lives); Aethelmaer (Aethelweard's son, who later founds Eynsham and supports Aelfric); Saint Edmund (An English king and martyr whose life is part of the collection)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aethelweard and his son Aethelmaer ask for more saints than the Homilies held.
Aelfric says the earlier books covered saints kept by all the English.
This set tells of saints honored by monks in their own services.
The pieces are meant for devout reading, not only for preaching.
The Life of Saint Edmund is one piece.
The style is rhythmical alliterative prose.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Beowulf

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 8th-10th century (Sort Year: 950)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Beowulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A hero fights Grendel, Grendel's mother, and a dragon.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 8th-11th century, manuscript c. 1000. The British Library dates the Nowell Codex, Cotton Vitellius A.xv, to about 1000. Scholars still dispute the year of composition. Many place the poem in the 8th to 10th centuries.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Beowulf (A Geatish hero who later becomes king); Hrothgar (King of the Danes, owner of the hall Heorot); Grendel (A monster who raids the hall at night); Grendel's mother (A lake monster who avenges her son); Wiglaf (The young warrior who stays for the dragon fight)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The monster Grendel attacks King Hrothgar's hall.
Beowulf sails from Geatland and tears off Grendel's arm.
Grendel's mother seeks revenge, and Beowulf kills her under the water.
Years later a dragon wakes, and the old king fights it.
Beowulf dies from the dragon's bite, and his people mourn him.

items.title: "Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (“Sermon of the Wolf to the English”)" (c. 1014) — Wulfstan

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (“Sermon of the Wolf to the English”)

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1014 (Sort Year: 1014)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Wulfstan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A fierce English sermon that blames national sin for the Viking terror.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: c. 1014 or 1016 confuses this sermon with a wrong death date. Wulfstan died in 1023. A rubric dates one revision to 1014, when the Danes harried the English most. The homily was composed and reworked between about 1010 and 1016. Ethelred returned from exile in 1014.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Wulfstan (Archbishop of York, preaching under the name Lupus, the wolf); The English (The hearers he charges with sin and calls back to God's law); King Ethelred (The king driven from his kingdom, named as a recent shame)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Wulfstan tells the English that the truth of their peril must be faced.
He says years of raid, hunger, and fire are the fruit of their sins.
He lists killings, broken oaths, slavery, and betrayal of one's lord.
He recalls King Edward murdered and King Ethelred driven from the land.
He warns that only repentance can turn aside a worse punishment.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Divine Comedy

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Dante Alighieri

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A pilgrim walks through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven during Easter week in 1300.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Digital Dante places the start of Inferno about 1308, Purgatorio around 1314, and Paradiso from about 1316. The poem was finished near his death in 1321. The story is set in 1300. It has three parts: Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dante the pilgrim (The poet as a traveler through the three worlds of the afterlife); Virgil (The Roman poet who guides him through Hell and Purgatory); Beatrice (The beloved who guides him through Heaven); Satan (The frozen giant at the center of Hell)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It has three parts:.
Inferno.
Purgortorio.
Paradiso.
It is written in 3 lined Terza Rima, in 100 Cantos (34 in Inferno, 33 each in Purgotorio and Paradiso).
The long epic Divine Comedy began in about 1308 and was finished just before Dante's death in 1321.
Main Theme: Life after death, Dante himself is the chief character in it.
Dante called it Comedia, because it ended happily.
In Inferno(Hell) there are 9 circles of hell named "Limbo, Lust, Gluttony, Greed, Anger, Heresy, Violence, Fraud and Treachery.
The paradise has 9 levels with Garden of Eden at the summit as a 10th level.
Inferno begins on the day before Good Friday in 1300, where Dante himself is the narrator.
On Good Friday he is rescued by Virgil.
In Inferno and Purgatorio, Dante is guided by Virgil and there he meets friends and foes.
Dante found Socrates, Heraclitus, Horace and Ovid in the first circle (Limbo) of hell, in this circle there were those who did not accept Christ and was thus unbaptized.
In Paradiso, Dante has a visions of world's beauty, light and sound where he is guided by Beatrice. She guides Dante through 10 spheres of heaven where he meets blessed souls.
He finally arrived at The Throne of God.
Dante stands in rapture and perceives the final truth of life and meaning of the universe.
In Purgotorio, a mountain rising in circular ledges on which there are various groups of repentant sinners and at the top of that mountain there is earthly paradise where Dante meets Beatrice.
Lost in a dark wood, the pilgrim meets the Roman poet Virgil.
Virgil leads him down through the nine circles of Hell.
They climb the mountain of Purgatory, where souls repent.
Beatrice replaces Virgil and leads him through the spheres of Heaven.
The journey ends in a vision of God as the love that moves the stars.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Historia Regum Britanniae

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1136 (Sort Year: 1136)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Geoffrey of Monmouth

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Latin account of British kings from Brutus of Troy through Arthur's reign.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: 1095 to c. 1155 is a life span, not the year of the book. The Welsh Biography says the History appeared at the start of 1136. Oxford Reference says about 1136. Dedications vary, often to Robert, earl of Gloucester. The Prophecies of Merlin were quoted by Orderic Vitalis in 1135.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Brutus (A descendant of Aeneas who begins the line of British kings); King Leir (A British king whose story later poets and playwrights retold); Merlin (The prophet whose sayings form a book inside the History); Arthur (The British king pictured as a national hero against the Saxons)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Geoffrey says Walter of Oxford gave him a very ancient British book.
The story starts with Brutus, a descendant of Aeneas, who settles the island.
Famous kings include Leir and Cymbeline, long before the Saxon age.
Merlin's prophecies fill a central section that had already circulated alone.
Arthur rises as the hero who defends Britain against the Saxons after Rome leaves.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ormulum

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Orm

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Gospel homilies in English verse, spelled so a reader knows each short vowel.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says about 1180 and stores 1180 as a birth year. That year is a working date. Wikipedia dates a finish about 1180. The Bodleian dates the manuscript to the 1170s or 1180s. Britannica prefers about 1200.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Orm (The canon who preaches and invents the spelling); Walter (Orm's brother and fellow canon, who asked for the book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Orm names the book Ormulum because Orm made it.
He writes at the request of his brother Walter.
Each homily paraphrases a Gospel passage for the Mass.
He then explains that passage for priests and lay hearers.
Doubled consonants show that the vowel before them is short.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Brut

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Layamon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long verse history of Britain, with a large section on King Arthur.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives late 12th to early 13th century, plus a false year 1250. Wikipedia dates the Brut about 1190. Britannica dates it about 1200. The span about 1190 to 1215 covers both.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Layamon (The priest narrator who names himself at the start); Brutus (The Trojan founder of Britain in the opening history); Arthur (The British war king who fills much of the poem); Merlin (The prophet whose birth and counsel enter the Arthur story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story starts with Brutus, descendant of the Trojan Aeneas.
It follows legendary British kings, including Lear and Merlin.
Arthur becomes the great war leader of the island.
Layamon tells how the Round Table was founded.
Arthur is carried toward Avalon to be healed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Havelok the Dane

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Beowulf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lost Danish prince grows up as a kitchen boy and wins two crowns.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says 13th century only. Skeat's edition title says about 1280, in the reign of Edward I. The full copy is Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Laud Misc. 108.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Havelok (The exiled prince of Denmark, raised as a poor boy); Grim (The fisherman who spares Havelok and flees to England); Goldborow (The English princess forced into marriage with Havelok); Godard (The Danish earl who tries to kill the royal children); Godrich (The English earl who seizes the throne from Goldborow)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Earl Godard orders the fisherman Grim to drown the boy Havelok.
Grim sees a light from the child's mouth and saves him.
Havelok works in Lincoln and is married to Princess Goldborow.
He wins Denmark, then returns and defeats Earl Godrich.
Havelok and Goldborow rule England in a long peace.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Confessio Amantis

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1390 (Sort Year: 1390)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Gower

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Amans confesses sins against love, and Genius answers with many tales.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives only the life span c. 1330-1408. Luminarium dates the first complete version to 1390, with praise of Richard II. Revisions of 1390-1393 shift the dedication to Henry of Lancaster. Wikipedia gives c. 1386-1393.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amans (The lover who confesses, and who is revealed as old John Gower); Genius (Priest of Venus, who hears the confession and tells the tales); Venus (The goddess who dismisses the lover at the end)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Prologue mourns division in the realm and in the church.
Amans, the lover, confesses to Genius, the priest of Venus.
Genius tells tales arranged by the seven deadly sins.
The stories join private love to lessons about rule.
A later version dedicates the book to Henry of Lancaster.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Mirour de l’Omme

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Gower

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long French poem on sin, the three estates, and the soul's reform.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives only the life span c. 1330-1408. Luminarium dates the Mirour to c. 1376-1379. Wikipedia gives the same French dates and the Latin title Speculum Meditantis. The ending of the sole manuscript is lost.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (The moral teacher who holds up a mirror to mankind); The Devil and Sin (The forces whose offspring fill the allegory of vice); The Virgin (The holy figure who leads the poem toward repentance)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem follows sin from the devil's fall into human life.
It maps the vices and the answering virtues.
It then rebukes the three estates of society.
It turns toward the Virgin and the path of repentance.
The close of the only manuscript has been lost.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Vox Clamantis

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1381 (Sort Year: 1381)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Gower

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Latin poem on the Peasants' Revolt and the sins of each estate.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives only the life span c. 1330-1408. Luminarium says Gower began the poem in 1377. The revolt book answers the rising of 1381. Wikipedia lists the Latin poem as c. 1377-1381.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Dreamer (The speaker who sees the revolt as a beast allegory); King Richard II (The young king whom the later books advise); William Walworth (The mayor whose blow ends the rebel leader in the poem)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Book 1 dreams the revolt of 1381 as a nightmare of beasts.
Rebels storm London, and William Walworth strikes their leader.
Later books attack the sins of priests, knights, and peasants.
The poem also gives counsel to the young King Richard II.
Gower kept revising the Latin after the revolt year.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Piers Plowman

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Langland

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Will dreams of a field of folk and searches for a true Christian life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives the life span c. 1332 to c. 1386, not separate poem dates. Luminarium places the A text around 1362 and the B text around 1377. The C text belongs to the 1380s. The Poetry Foundation dates the A text by about 1370.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Will (The dreamer whose visions make up the poem); Piers the Plowman (The honest plowman who guides the folk toward Truth); Lady Meed (The figure of reward and bribery, tried before the king); Holy Church (The teacher who first explains Truth to Will); Conscience (The figure who opposes Lady Meed and later guides the search)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Will sleeps by the Malvern Hills and sees a field full of folk.
Holy Church teaches him, and Lady Meed is brought before the king.
The Seven Deadly Sins confess, and Piers sets the people to work.
A pardon comes from Truth, then Will seeks Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest.
Later dreams show Christ's harrowing of hell and a church under attack.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Canzoniere

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Petrarch

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book of 366 Italian poems, mostly sonnets, on the poet's love for Laura.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Poems begin soon after the meeting with Laura in 1327. The latest new poems are about 1368. He kept arranging the book until his death in 1374. Another title is Rime Sparse (Scattered Rhymes). The Latin title is Rerum vulgarium fragmenta.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Petrarch the speaker (The poet who records love, guilt, and spiritual change); Laura (The beloved woman, alive in the early poems and mourned after 1348)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The opening sonnet speaks to readers of scattered rhymes.
Petrarch recalls first seeing Laura at Avignon in 1327.
He praises her beauty, and he also confesses restless desire.
After Laura dies in 1348, the poems turn to grief and prayer.
He orders the whole book as the story of one soul.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Cleanness

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: late 14th century (Sort Year: 1350)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Gawain Poet

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Bible stories warn that God honors the pure and punishes filth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Cleanness, also called Purity, is the second poem in Cotton Nero A.x. The book is late 14th century. It is a biblical poem on cleanness, not a romance.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (The teacher who links courtesy with spiritual cleanness); Noah (The man spared when God floods a filthy world); Belshazzar (The king whose feast defiles the temple vessels)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet says the clean of heart are fit to see God.
He warns that pride and filth bring down God's anger.
The Flood and the fall of Sodom show ruined sinners.
Belshazzar's feast shows a king who soils holy vessels.
The poem calls for cleanness of body, worship, and soul.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Decameron

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Giovanni Boccaccio

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ten young people flee the Florence plague and tell one hundred stories in ten days.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Brown chronology dates the main writing to 1349-1351. Britannica Kids gives the wider span 1348-1353. The tales are set during the Florence plague of 1348. He kept revising the book later. The name means ten days.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pampinea (The woman who first proposes the country retreat and the storytelling); Dioneo (A young man often allowed to tell a freer, more comic tale); Fiammetta (One of the seven women in the storytelling group); Panfilo (One of the three young men in the group)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Contains 100 stories told over 10 days.
7 young women and 3 young men flee Florance during the Black Death and take refuge for 2 weeks in the countryside.
They spent hot afternoons by telling stories .
Each day the group selects a King or Queen who determines the general theme of stories of that day.
Theme of the first day of storytelling is "Free to choose".
The preface describes the Black Death in Florence in 1348.
Seven women and three men leave the city for a country villa.
Each day one of them rules, and each person tells one tale.
The tales move from tricks and grief to happy love and noble acts.
On the tenth day they tell of generous deeds, then return to Florence.

items.title: "English Bible associated with the Wycliffite translations" (c. 1382-1395) — John Wycliffe

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: English Bible associated with the Wycliffite translations

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Wycliffe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The first full English Bible made from the Latin Vulgate, in two main versions.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates these versions from about 1382 to 1395. The Later Version came several years after Wycliffe died in 1384. A 1408 Oxford ruling then restricted new English Bibles.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Wycliffe (The reformer whose circle is linked with the project); Nicholas of Hereford (Named as translator up to a point in the Early Version); John Purvey (The follower usually linked with the Later Version)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Translators worked from the Latin Bible, not from Hebrew or Greek.
The Early Version, about 1382, keeps Latin word order.
A note in one copy names Nicholas of Hereford, then other men.
The Later Version uses smoother English and is tied to John Purvey.
That later form was finished about 1395, after Wycliffe had died.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Mandeville's Travels

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1357 (Sort Year: 1357)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Mandeville

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A supposed knight reports travels from Europe to the Holy Land and beyond.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica places the French book about 1356 to 1357. Wikipedia gives writing between 1357 and 1371. The oldest dated manuscript is from 1371.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir John Mandeville (The narrator, presented as a knight of St Albans); The Sultan of Egypt (A ruler the narrator claims to have met); The Great Khan (The ruler of Cathay in the chapters on China); Prester John (A legendary Christian king placed in the far East)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator calls himself a knight from St Albans.
He says he left England in 1322 and traveled for many years.
The first part follows routes toward Jerusalem.
Later chapters add India, China, and strange creatures.
Scholars trace those wonders to older books, not to one journey.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Patience

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: late 14th century (Sort Year: 1350)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Gawain Poet

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The poem retells Jonah to teach patience under God's will.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem is the third item in Cotton Nero A.x, a late 14th century manuscript. Its story is the whole Book of Jonah, expanded in Middle English verse.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (The preacher who links patience to the Beatitudes); Jonah (The prophet who runs from God and then complains); God (The patient lord who spares Nineveh)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet praises patience as a blessed virtue.
God sends Jonah to warn the city of Nineveh.
Jonah flees by ship, and the sailors cast him into the sea.
A great fish swallows him, and he prays in its belly.
Nineveh repents, and Jonah must stop sulking at God's mercy.

items.title: "Printed Le Morte Darthur and his own prefaces" (1490) — William Caxton

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Printed Le Morte Darthur and his own prefaces

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1490 (Sort Year: 1490)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Caxton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Caxton's prefaces discuss English usage, Chaucer, and the books he chose to print.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: This entry is the preface group. The Eneydos prologue, with egges and eyren, is dated 1490. The first Canterbury Tales printing is about 1476-1477. The Morte preface belongs to the 31 July 1485 edition, also listed under its own slug.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William Caxton (The printer who speaks in his own prefaces about English); The merchant (A mercer who asks a housewife for egges and is not understood); The good wife (The woman who knows the word eyren, not egges)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He wrote prefaces and epilogues for many of his printed books.
He printed Chaucer's Canterbury Tales at Westminster about 1476.
He later printed a revised Canterbury Tales, using a better copy.
In the Eneydos preface of 1490 he tells the egges and eyren story.
A merchant asked for egges, and a woman understood only the word eyren.

items.title: "Revelations of Divine Love" (1670) — Julian of Norwich

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Revelations of Divine Love

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1670 (Sort Year: 1670)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Julian of Norwich

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sixteen visions of Christ's love, told first briefly and then at length.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The visions came in May 1373. Britannica places the longer account 20 or 30 years later. Wikipedia allows a finished long text in the early 1400s. Serenus de Cressy printed that long text in 1670.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Julian (The writer who receives and explains the showings); Christ (The speaker of the visions, also described as a mother); Mary (Christ's mother, present in the early showings)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Julian falls very ill and is given the last rites.
She sees Christ suffer and receives sixteen showings.
The short text records the visions soon afterward.
The long text later adds long thoughts on sin and love.
Christ answers her fear about sin.
All shall be well.

items.title: "The Book of Margery Kempe" (1501) — Margery Kempe

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Book of Margery Kempe

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1501 (Sort Year: 1501)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Margery Kempe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dictated life of illness, visions, tears, marriage, and long pilgrimages.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The priest began his rewrite on 23 July 1436. Book II began on 28 April 1438. Extracts were printed about 1501. A modernized full text appeared in 1936, and the Middle English edition in 1940.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Margery Kempe (The visionary, called this creature, who dictates the life); John Kempe (Her husband, who agrees to a chaste marriage); Jesus Christ (The divine speaker who comforts and commands her); Julian of Norwich (The anchoress who hears her story and offers counsel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After her first child she falls ill and sees Christ.
She later seeks a chaste marriage and a life of prayer.
She travels to Jerusalem, Rome, and other holy places.
She visits Julian of Norwich and is encouraged.
A priest rewrites the book from 1436, and Book II starts in 1438.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Fall of Princes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1494 (Sort Year: 1494)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Lydgate

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A huge book of tragedies, from Adam to near Lydgate's own age, written for Duke Humphrey.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Poetry Foundation dates the writing 1431-1439. Exam lists often use 1431-1438. The source is a French prose version of Boccaccio's De Casibus. The same poem is also stored as john-lydgate-fall-of-princes. First print is 1494.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Lydgate (The monk narrator who moralizes each fall); Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester (The patron who asked for envoys teaching princes by other men's falls); Fortune (The power that throws people from high rank to misery)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, asks for an English book of famous falls.
Lydgate works from a French prose version of Boccaccio's De Casibus.
He begins with Adam and Eve and moves through biblical and classical lives.
After many tragedies he adds an envoy of advice to princes.
He ends the long work with falls close to his own century.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Pearl

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: late 14th century (Sort Year: 1350)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Gawain Poet

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A father dreams of his dead child, who teaches him from heaven.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says 14th century. It is the first poem in Cotton Nero A.x, a late 14th century book. The poem is a dream vision and an elegy for a dead child. No separate print date is fixed in the sources opened here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Dreamer (The grieving father who lost his young child); The Pearl maiden (His dead child, now a queen and bride of the Lamb); The Lamb (Christ, seen in the heavenly city with a wounded side)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A father grieves in a garden for his lost pearl, a dead child.
He sleeps and sees a bright land beyond a river.
The Pearl maiden teaches him about grace and equal heavenly reward.
She shows him the New Jerusalem and the Lamb.
He tries to cross the water, wakes, and turns toward Christ.

items.title: "Sir Gawain and the Green Knight" (1839) — Anonymous — Gawain Poet

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1839 (Sort Year: 1839)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Gawain Poet

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sir Gawain takes a beheading challenge and is tested for a year.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says 14th century. Luminarium places composition in the mid to late 14th century. Madden first printed the poem in 1839. The only copy is British Library MS Cotton Nero A.x.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir Gawain (Arthur's nephew, who bears the pentangle and then the green girdle); The Green Knight (The challenger, later revealed as the host Bertilak); Lady Bertilak (The host's wife, who tempts Gawain in his bedroom); Morgan le Fay (The enchantress who sends the Green Knight to test the court); King Arthur (The king at Camelot who lets Gawain take the challenge)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A green knight enters Camelot and offers a beheading game.
Gawain cuts off his head, and the knight picks it up.
The knight tells Gawain to meet him at the Green Chapel in a year.
At a castle Gawain hides a green girdle and breaks the exchange game.
The Green Knight nicks his neck, and Gawain returns in shame.

items.title: "traditionally associated with Pearl" (late 14th century) — Anonymous — Gawain Poet

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: traditionally associated with Pearl

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: late 14th century (Sort Year: 1350)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anonymous — Gawain Poet

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A database label for the four poems grouped in Cotton Nero A.x.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database title, traditionally associated with Pearl, is a broken phrase from a Gawain note. It is not an independent text. The four real poems sit together in British Library MS Cotton Nero A.x.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The database split a descriptive note into this extra row.
It is not a fifth poem by the Gawain Poet.
Pearl, Cleanness, Patience, and Sir Gawain share one manuscript.
Many scholars treat one poet as the maker of all four.
Some studies still ask whether Pearl had a different poet.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Dialogue with a Friend

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A friend questions Hoccleve's recovery and urges him to write again.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span as the work date. Luminarium dates the Dialogue about 1420-1421. ARLIMA dates the whole Series, Complaint plus Dialogue, between 1419 and 1421. It is not a separate prose essay.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Hoccleve (The poet who defends his recovered wits); The Friend (A visitor who doubts him, then gives him work to do)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A friend visits and finds Hoccleve writing the Complaint.
The friend fears that new writing will bring back the illness.
Hoccleve says his wits have returned and that work will prove it.
The friend then sets him literary tasks, including a moral tale.
The dialogue joins the Complaint to the rest of the Series.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: La Male Regle

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic petition in which Hoccleve confesses bad habits and asks for overdue pay.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints his life dates, 1367-1426, as the work date. Luminarium dates the poem about 1405. EBSCO dates it 1406. The usual exam range is about 1405-1406. The title means the bad rule.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Hoccleve (The clerk who confesses misrule and asks for his fee); The Lord Treasurer (The officer who can release the poet's overdue pay)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet addresses the Lord Treasurer about his unpaid salary.
He confesses nights in Westminster taverns and costly clothes.
He jokes that this bad rule has hurt his health and his purse.
He asks that the overdue payment be released.
The poem turns a begging letter into a self portrait.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Complaint

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Hoccleve describes a mental illness and the loneliness that followed his recovery.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span 1367-1426 as the work date. ARLIMA dates the Series, which begins with this Complaint, between 1419 and 1421. John Burrow places the Complaint about 1420. It is also called My Compleinte.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Hoccleve (The speaker who describes his illness and his return to health); Reason (A figure in the consoling book he reads during the poem)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After harvest, the poet looks into a mirror of memory.
He recalls a time when his wits failed him.
Friends now doubt that his mind has truly returned.
He finds comfort in a book of a sorrowing man and Reason.
The poem opens the Series, his late group of linked works.

items.title: "The Complaint of the Black Knight" (c. 1402) — John Lydgate

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Complaint of the Black Knight

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1402 (Sort Year: 1402)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Lydgate

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dream poem in which a knight in black laments his unreturned love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span as the work date. The Poetry Foundation groups it with courtly poems of the first decade. The Temple of Glass is dated there 1403. The usual early date is about 1402. It is an early Chaucerian dream poem, not a later public chronicle.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet dreamer (The narrator who overhears the knight and records his complaint); The Black Knight (A lover in black who grieves for a lady who does not love him back)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet walks out on a May morning among flowers and birds.
He hears a sorrowing knight dressed in black.
The knight complains that his lady will not return his love.
The poet wakes and writes the complaint down.
The poem echoes Chaucer's dream visions and the Knight in Black.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Story of Thebes

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Lydgate

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lydgate joins Chaucer's pilgrims and tells the story of Thebes on the way home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span as the work date. The Poetry Foundation dates the poem 1420-1422 and also says about 1421. It is meant as the first tale on the ride home from Canterbury. It answers the Knight's Tale and runs to 4,716 lines.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Lydgate (The monk who joins the pilgrims and tells the tale); Harry Bailly (Chaucer's Host, who asks Lydgate for the first homeward tale); Oedipus (The Theban king whose family crime begins the disaster); Eteocles and Polyneices (The brothers who kill each other in the war for Thebes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
vi) Fall of Prince (1438) - 30,000 lines on Monk's Tale.
The monk arrives at Canterbury and meets Harry Bailly.
The Host invites him to tell the first tale on the return.
Lydgate tells how Oedipus came to rule Thebes.
The sons Eteocles and Polyneices destroy each other in the siege.
The story ends where Chaucer's Knight's Tale begins, with the unburied dead.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Temple of Glass

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Lydgate

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dreamer visits a temple of glass and hears two lovers plead before Venus.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span as the work date. The Poetry Foundation marks the poem 1403, with a question mark. Later scholars have also proposed other years. Caxton printed it at Westminster about 1476-1477. The lady's motto, De mieulx en mieulx, means from better to better.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The dreamer (The poet who enters the temple and records the lovers' pleas); Venus (The goddess who hears the lovers and promises aid); The lady (A woman in the dream who asks Venus for relief); The knight (The male lover who pleads in the temple)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator falls asleep and dreams of a temple of glass.
Inside, unhappy lovers complain before the goddess Venus.
A lady and a knight each pray for relief in love.
Venus promises help, and the motto is De mieulx en mieulx.
The dreamer wakes and writes the vision for other lovers.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Troy Book

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1513 (Sort Year: 1513)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Lydgate

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long verse history of Troy, written for Prince Henry and finished in 1420.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span as the work date. Lydgate began the poem in 1412 for Prince Henry and finished it in 1420. It runs to about 30,000 lines. Pynson's printed edition of 1513 uses the title of the siege and destruction of Troy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prince Henry (The patron, later Henry V, who commissioned the poem in 1412); Lydgate the narrator (The monk who retells the Trojan history and adds moral comment); Troilus (The Trojan prince whose love story Chaucer had already told)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Prince Henry asks Lydgate for an English history of Troy.
Lydgate follows Guido delle Colonne, not Homer's Greek epic.
He tells the causes of the war, the siege, and the fall of the city.
He includes the love of Troilus, already famous from Chaucer.
He finishes in 1420, when the prince has become King Henry V.

items.title: "The Book of the Duchess" (1532) — Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Book of the Duchess

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1532 (Sort Year: 1532)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dream vision elegy mourning the death of Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Composed c. 1368-1369 after the death of Blanche of Lancaster on 12 September 1368 (or 1369). First printed in William Thynne's 1532 edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dreamer (The sleepless narrator who listens to the mourning knight); Knight in Black (A grieving knight representing John of Gaunt); Lady White (The deceased beloved wife representing Blanche of Lancaster)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator cannot sleep and reads the story of Ceyx and Alcyone.
He falls asleep and dreams of a May morning and a royal hunt.
In the woods he meets a grieving Knight in Black.
The Knight tells how he loved and lost his lady named White.
The dreamer realizes the lady is dead and wakes up.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Canterbury Tales

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A frame narrative of 24 stories told by pilgrims riding from the Tabard Inn in Southwark to the shrine of St. Thomas Becket in Canterbury.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Composed between c. 1387 and Chaucer's death in 1400. Contains 24 tales by 23 pilgrims. First printed by William Caxton c. 1476-1478.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Knight; Alisoun (The Wife of Bath); Harry Bailly (The Host); The Pardoner; Madame Eglantine (The Prioress); The Parson & The Plowman

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
1. The General Prologue (858 lines in Heroic Couplets) opens in April ('Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote') as pilgrims travel to the shrine of martyr St. Thomas Becket at Canterbury.
2. The Knight's Tale (Source: Boccaccio's Teseida): Duke Theseus of Athens defeats Creon of Thebes and imprisons two Theban royal cousins, Palamon and Arcite. Both fall in love with Theseus's sister-in-law Emily. Palamon prays to Venus, Arcite to Mars, and Emily to Diana. Arcite wins the tournament, but Saturn causes his horse to throw him; dying, Arcite commends Palamon to Emily.
3. The Miller's Tale (Fabliau): Drunken Miller Robin interrupts the Monk. Young Oxford astrology student Nicholas tricks old carpenter John into hanging three wooden tubs from the roof for a fake 'second Noah's Flood' so Nicholas can sleep with John's young wife Alison. Parish clerk Absolon takes revenge with a hot iron poker; Nicholas shouts 'Water!', and John cuts the rope and breaks his arm.
4. The Reeve's Tale (Fabliau): Offended because he is a carpenter himself, Oswald the Reeve tells how two Cambridge students (John and Aleyn) get even with dishonest Miller Symkyn of Trumpington who stole their flour.
5. The Cook's Tale: Roger the Cook begins a bawdy London story about a reveling apprentice named Perkyn Reveller, but it breaks off unfinished after 58 lines.
6. The Man of Law's Tale (Rhyme Royal): Tells the Christian romance of Constance (Custance), daughter of the Roman Emperor, who endures two wicked mothers-in-law (the Sultaness of Syria and Donegild of Northumberland) and years adrift on a rudderless ship before reuniting with King Alla.
7. The Wife of Bath's Prologue & Tale: Alisoun defends marriage and female experience across her five husbands (three old and rich, two young including Oxford clerk Jankyn). Her Arthurian tale follows a knight who must discover what women desire most; a loathly old hag reveals the answer ('sovereignty' over their husbands and lovers) and transforms into a faithful young beauty when given the choice.
8. The Friar's Tale: Friar Huberd tells how a corrupt, extorting church Summoner meets a Yeoman who is actually a devil from hell, and is dragged to hell when an old widow curses him from the heart.
9. The Summoner's Tale: In furious retaliation, the Summoner describes 20,000 friars nesting under Satan's tail in hell and tells how greedy Friar John is humiliated by a sick peasant named Thomas.
10. The Clerk's Tale (Rhyme Royal, from Petrarch's Latin version of Boccaccio): Walter, Marquis of Saluzzo, marries the poor peasant girl Patient Griselda and subjects her to cruel trials (pretending to kill their two children and stage a new marriage), which she endures with unbroken patience.
11. The Merchant's Tale: Old blind knight January marries young May, who betrays him up in a pear tree with squire Damian while Pluto and Proserpina debate.
12. The Squire's Tale (Unfinished Oriental Romance): Set at the court of Mongol ruler Cambyuskan (Genghis Khan), featuring four magical gifts: a flying brass horse, a truth-revealing mirror, a sword that heals and wounds, and a ring taught to princess Canacee that lets her understand the speech of a heartbroken falcon.
13. The Franklin's Tale (Breton Lay): Dorigen rashly promises squire Aurelius her love if he removes the dangerous black rocks on the coast of Brittany; when a magician creates the illusion that the rocks are gone, her husband Arveragus insists she keep her word, inspiring Aurelius and the magician to forgive the debt in a contest of generosity.
14. The Physician's Tale (from Livy and Roman de la Rose): Corrupt Roman judge Appius conspires with Claudius to claim pure Virginia as a runaway slave; her father Virginius slays her to preserve her honor.
15. The Pardoner's Prologue & Tale ('Radix malorum est cupiditas' - Greed is the root of all evil): Three rioters set out to kill 'Death', find eight bushels of gold coins under an oak tree, and murder one another with stabs and poisoned wine.
16. The Shipman's Tale: A monk borrows 100 francs from a merchant of Saint-Denis and gives those exact coins to the merchant's wife in exchange for a night together.
17. The Prioress's Tale (Rhyme Royal): A miracle of the Virgin Mary about a seven-year-old Christian choirboy ('little clergeon') who continues singing Alma Redemptoris Mater even after his throat is cut.
18. Chaucer's Tale of Sir Thopas: A hilarious tail-rhyme parody of bad medieval knightly romances about Sir Thopas seeking an elf-queen, until Harry Bailly stops Chaucer ('Thy drasty rymyng is nat worth a toord!').
19. Chaucer's Tale of Melibee (Prose): A long moral prose allegory in which wise Dame Prudence persuades her husband Melibee to forgive the three enemies who attacked their daughter Sophie.
20. The Monk's Tale (8-line stanzas): 17 brief tragic 'falls of illustrious men' (De Casibus tragedies) from Lucifer, Adam, Samson, and Hercules to Julius Caesar and Croesus, interrupted by the Knight.
21. The Nun's Priest's Tale (Mock-Heroic Beast Fable, from Roman de Renart): Proud rooster Chauntecleer ignores his prophetic dream (and wife Pertelote's laxative advice), is captured through flattery by Don Russell the Fox, and escapes by tricking the fox into opening his mouth to boast.
22. The Second Nun's Tale (Rhyme Royal): The hagiography (saint's life) and martyrdom of Saint Cecilia and her husband Valerian.
23. The Canon's Yeoman's Tale: After the alchemist Canon flees in fear of exposure, his Yeoman reveals the frauds of alchemy.
24. The Manciple's Tale (from Ovid's Metamorphoses): How Phoebus Apollo's pet white crow told him of his wife Coronis's infidelity, causing Phoebus to kill his wife in anger and turn all crows black.
25. The Parson's Tale (Prose Treatise) & Chaucer's Retraction: As evening falls near Canterbury, the virtuous Parson delivers a long prose sermon on Penitence and the Seven Deadly Sins, followed by Chaucer's Retraction asking forgiveness for his secular works.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The House of Fame

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1484 (Sort Year: 1484)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dream vision poem where an eagle carries the narrator to the palace of Fame.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives 'c. 1340s-1400'. Composed during Chaucer's customs comptroller period, c. 1379-1384 (Skeat suggests 1383-1384). Left unfinished at line 2158. First printed by William Caxton in 1484.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Geffrey (The bookish narrator and dreamer); The Eagle (A giant golden bird sent by Jupiter who speaks with comic authority); Lady Fame (The capricious ruler who gives arbitrary renown to people)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Chaucer falls asleep and finds himself in a glass temple of Venus.
A giant golden eagle carries him high up into the heavens.
The eagle talks humorously and explains how sound travels to Fame's dwelling.
Chaucer sees Lady Fame grant glory or slander unfairly to applicants.
He visits the whirling House of Rumor, but the poem breaks off unfinished.

items.title: "The Legend of Good Women" (1532) — Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Legend of Good Women

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1532 (Sort Year: 1532)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A collection of stories praising faithful women who suffered for love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives 'c. 1340s-1400'. Composed c. 1385-1387; Prologue revised c. 1394-1395 after Queen Anne died. Left incomplete with nine legends. First printed in William Thynne's 1532 edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Narrator / Chaucer (The poet performing penance for his past writings on love); God of Love (Cupid) (The angry king who rebukes Chaucer for slandering lovers); Queen Alceste (The merciful queen who intercedes for Chaucer); Cleopatra, Thisbe, Dido (Famous heroines whose tragic loyalty to love is narrated)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet praises the daisy flower on a lovely May day.
The God of Love accuses Chaucer of writing against women in Troilus.
Queen Alceste defends Chaucer and assigns him a penance.
He must write legends celebrating women who stayed true in love.
Chaucer narrates nine legends before leaving the planned twenty stories unfinished.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Parliament of Fowls

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1478 (Sort Year: 1478)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Birds gather on Valentine's Day before the goddess Nature to choose their mates.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives 'c. 1340s-1400'. Composed c. 1381-1382 to celebrate the marriage negotiations between King Richard II and Anne of Bohemia. First printed by William Caxton in 1478.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Narrator (The poet studying love through old books); Nature (The noble goddess presiding over all living creatures); Formel Eagle (The graceful female eagle sought by three royal suitors); Africanus (Scipio the elder who guides the dreamer into the garden)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator reads Scipio's Dream and falls asleep.
Africanus guides him into a beautiful garden of love.
Birds assemble on Valentine's Day before the goddess Nature.
Three royal eagles compete for the love of a noble female eagle.
The other birds debate noisily, and the choice is postponed for one year.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Troilus and Criseyde

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1483 (Sort Year: 1483)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragic romance of two lovers during the Trojan War, broken by betrayal and politics.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Composed in the mid-1380s (c. 1382-1386). Dedicated to John Gower and Ralph Strode. First printed by William Caxton in 1483.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Troilus (A noble Trojan prince and faithful lover); Criseyde (A prudent Trojan widow who later yields to Diomede); Pandarus (Criseyde's witty uncle and go-between friend to Troilus); Diomede (The smooth-talking Greek warrior who wins Criseyde)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Troilus falls deeply in love with the Trojan widow Criseyde.
Pandarus helps Troilus woo and secretly unite with Criseyde.
Criseyde is traded to the Greek camp in exchange for Antenor.
In the Greek camp, Diomede persuades Criseyde to accept his love.
Troilus dies in battle and looks down laughing at earthly sorrow.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Regiment of Princes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1411 (Sort Year: 1411)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long advice poem for Prince Henry, with a prologue about the poet's worries.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Luminarium and EBSCO place the poem in 1411, for Henry, Prince of Wales. It draws on the Secretum Secretorum tradition and on Giles of Rome. The famous Chaucer portrait is in British Library Harley MS 4866.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Hoccleve (The anxious clerk who writes the book for the prince); The old man (A beggar who talks with Hoccleve in the prologue); Prince Henry (The future Henry V, the prince addressed by the poem); Geoffrey Chaucer (The dead master praised in the poem and pictured in one manuscript)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A poor and anxious Hoccleve walks out and meets an old man.
The old man advises him and tells moral stories.
Hoccleve then offers a book of rule to Prince Henry.
He praises Chaucer as his master and the flower of eloquence.
In Harley MS 4866 a portrait of Chaucer stands beside that praise.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Le Morte Darthur

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1485 (Sort Year: 1485)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Malory

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The rise and fall of King Arthur and the Round Table.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives the life span c. 1415-1471. Malory finished the book in the ninth year of Edward IV, 1469-1470. William Caxton printed it in 1485. Walter Oakeshott found the Winchester Manuscript in 1934. It is now British Library Additional MS 59678.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: King Arthur (The king who founds the Round Table and dies in the last battle); Guinevere (Arthur's queen, loved by Lancelot); Lancelot (The greatest knight, whose love splits the fellowship); Galahad (Lancelot's son, who achieves the Grail); Mordred (The traitor who seizes the realm and fights Arthur)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a compilation of traditional tales about the Legend King Arthur, Guinevere, Lancelot, and the Knights of the Round Table.
First published in 1485 by William Caxton.
Malory wrote about Arthur in 8 books but Caxton converted it into 21 books.
The books are: Book 1 : "From the Marriage of King Uther unto King Arthur that Reigned after Him and did Many Battles" Book 2 : "The Noble Tale Between King Arthur and Lucius the Emperor of Rome" Book 3 : "The Noble Tale of Sir Launcelot du Lake" Book 4 : "The Tale of Sir Gareth of Orkney" Book 5 : "The Book of Sir Tristram de Lyones" Book 6 : "The Noble Tale of the Sangreal" Book 7 : "Sir Launcelot and Queen Guinevere" Book 8 : "The Death of Arthur".
Arthur is proved king and gathers the knights of the Round Table.
The knights ride on quests, including the quest of the Holy Grail.
Lancelot's love for Guinevere breaks the fellowship.
Mordred rebels, and Arthur falls in the last battle.
Arthur is carried toward Avalon, and some say he will return.

items.title: "Introduced printing press to England in 1476" (1476) — William Caxton

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Introduced printing press to England in 1476

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1476 (Sort Year: 1476)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Caxton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Caxton brought printing to Westminster in 1476, after printing English books abroad.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database uses his life dates, about 1422-1491, for this item. The English press at Westminster dates from 1476. The Recuyell, the first printed English book, is placed about 1473-1474, often at Bruges. The Dictes is the early Westminster book of 1477. An indulgence of 13 December 1476 is an early English print.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He learned printing on the Continent and set up a press.
He printed the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye about 1473-1474.
That Troy book is the first book printed in English.
In 1476 he began printing at Westminster, near the Abbey.
In 1477 he printed The Dictes or Sayengis of the Philosophres there.

items.title: "printed Le Morte Darthur in 1485" (1485) — William Caxton

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: printed Le Morte Darthur in 1485

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1485 (Sort Year: 1485)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Caxton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Caxton printed Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur at Westminster on 31 July 1485.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives only Caxton's life span. The colophon date is 31 July 1485, at Westminster. Caxton split Malory's work into 21 books. The Winchester manuscript, found in 1934, keeps a different, eight part order.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: King Arthur (The king whose rise, Round Table, and fall fill the book); Sir Lancelot (Arthur's greatest knight and the lover of Queen Guinevere); Queen Guinevere (Arthur's queen, whose love for Lancelot helps break the court); William Caxton (The printer and editor who adds the 1485 preface)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Noble readers asked Caxton for the history of King Arthur.
He edited Sir Thomas Malory's Arthurian prose.
He divided the book into 21 books and many chapters.
He finished the printing at Westminster on 31 July 1485.
His preface tells the reader to follow virtue and leave vice.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Colin Clout

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1522 (Sort Year: 1522)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Skelton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Colin Clout, a plain spokesman, attacks corruption in the Church and Wolsey's pride.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span as the work date. The Poetry Foundation dates Colin Clout to 1522, after Speak, Parrot. The name Collyn Cloute is Skelton's. Edmund Spenser later reuses Colin Clout in The Shepheardes Calender. The poem attacks Church corruption and Wolsey.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Colin Clout (The plain wandering voice of common complaint); Cardinal Wolsey (The powerful cardinal blamed for pride and for harm to the Church)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Colin walks about and reports what common people are saying.
He attacks lazy, greedy, and ignorant clergy.
The blame gathers on Cardinal Wolsey, prelate and statesman.
He mentions the closing of small religious houses.
The rough short lines make the attack sound like common speech.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Phyllyp Sparowe

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1505 (Sort Year: 1505)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Skelton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mock elegy, in Skeltonic verse, for Jane Scrope's pet sparrow slain at Carrow.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span as the work date. The poem belongs to his years as rector of Diss, after 1504. It is usually dated about 1505. Jane Scrope lived with her mother at the Benedictine priory of Carrow, near Norwich. The title spelling Phyllyp Sparowe is Skelton's.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jane Scrope (The young woman at Carrow whose sparrow has been killed); Philip Sparrow (Jane's pet bird, the subject of the mock funeral); John Skelton (The poet who speaks the commendation and the later reply)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jane Scrope, a girl at Carrow Priory, mourns her pet sparrow.
The poem opens on the Placebo of the Office of the Dead.
She asks prayers for the soul of Philip Sparrow.
Birds gather for a comic requiem, and a cat is the killer.
Skelton then praises Jane and answers readers who mocked the poem.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Speke, Parrot

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1521 (Sort Year: 1521)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Skelton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A parrot in a cage speaks a coded satire against Cardinal Wolsey.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database prints the life span as the work date. The Poetry Foundation dates Speak, Parrot to 1521. It was written in layers and survives in partial texts that editors must join. Later collections printed it after Skelton's death. The posthumous tag in the database belongs more truly to later printings, not to the Bowge of Court.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Parrot (The caged bird whose broken, learned speech carries the satire); Galathea (The woman who asks Parrot to sing); Cardinal Wolsey (The powerful minister attacked under figures such as Moloch)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Parrot introduces himself as a learned, mimic bird.
He scatters Latin, proverb, and riddle so the attack is partly hidden.
The poem aims at Cardinal Wolsey's pride and power.
It also mocks the showy new learning of the humanists.
Later envoys grow plainer about Wolsey's political danger.
